1: Chapter 1: A Visitor on a Rainy Night

The rain in Ishikawa had been falling for three days now. Haruka Sato's older sister had left for the capital in the spring, and since then, the small pharmacy in town had been run entirely by Haruka alone.
When the sun went down, she closed the shutters, counted the day's earnings, blew out the light, and went upstairs to the second floor.
The moment she lay down, she heard fierce pounding on the door below, and a man's voice called out, "Is anyone there?"

In the doorway stood a young man, soaked to the bone. Blood had seeped through the cloth wrapped around his left arm. He gave his name as Ken'ichi Mori and said he was a member of the Azure Dragon Society.
"I'd like you to treat my wound," Mori said in a low voice. "I'll pay you. Will thirty-five hundred yen be enough?"
Mori took a letter wrapped in oil paper from inside his coat. "This letter must be delivered to Seifu by May eighteenth."
Haruka sighed inwardly. It was the season for gathering medicinal herbs, and she was so busy she could have used an extra pair of hands.
Still, Haruka did not take the money. She simply said, "First thing tomorrow morning, I'll guide you into the mountains."
2: As soon as dawn broke, the two set out. Haruka carried a basket on her back; inside were rice balls, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.

On the mountainside they met Shigeru Tanaka, an old man chopping firewood. He set down his axe and spoke in a hushed voice. Yesterday evening, he said, three strangers had been going around asking about a young man injured at the entrance to town.
"Haruka, take the back road," Tanaka said. "The main road is dangerous." Haruka thanked him.
The back road was narrow and slippery. Haruka went first, planting each step firmly as she went. Mori followed silently behind.

By midday the rain had stopped, the mountain mist slowly cleared, and in the distance the roof of Seifu appeared. A nun stood before the gate. It was a woman named Shizuka Yamamoto, who received guests at the temple.
Yamamoto took the letter, checked the red seal on the envelope, and nodded. "The abbot has been waiting for this letter for two years."
Mori said to Haruka, "You saved my life." Haruka smiled and replied, "Then next time you come, fix the roof of the apothecary." Mori stayed behind at the temple.
That evening, Haruka went down the mountain alone. By the time she reached home it was already dark; she lit a lamp and sat for a long time in the back of the shop.
